items.title: Best video color grading software in 2026 includes Adobe Premiere
items.content_html:
Professional color grading software can make or break the look of a video, and Adobe Premiere gives everyone from novices to seasoned professionals the tools to achieve cinematic results.

Capturing the video you need for a project is only half of the battle. Sometimes the footage you capture matches your creative vision with minimal editing, but when it isn't quite right, color grading can get you the rest of the way.

While some entry-level video editing tools rely heavily on basic filters, professional color grading software provides greater control over color, contrast, exposure, and tonal adjustments.

Adobe Premiere has an extensive suite of color grading tools baked in, with much of the work accomplished using the dedicated Color Mode. Support for third-party plug-ins provides even more creative flexibility.

Get Adobe Premiere

You don't need years of video editing experience to get started with Adobe Premiere. At the same time, its color grading tools offer enough depth to accommodate demanding professional workflows.

Color Management and Color Mode

Recording video in RAW or using a log color profile can give you greater flexibility during post-production. Adobe Premiere's built-in Color Management system simplifies the process, while Color Mode provides the tools needed to fine-tune your footage.

Color grading can transform an ordinary shot into cinematic footage. Adobe Premiere gives you precise control over color, contrast, and exposure, helping you preserve detail while achieving your desired aesthetic.

If you've ever wondered exactly how a Western achieves its sepia tone or your favorite sci-fi film has those cold corridors, it's thanks to color grading. What's great is that Adobe Premiere gives you as much artistic control as you want through direct manipulation or presets.

You can even import your own presets to create a specific look. Built-in tools like Auto Color can automatically adjust exposure and white balance, giving you a starting point for further creative refinements without sacrificing artistic control.

The best video color grading software provides the tools you need while staying out of the way. Adobe Premiere's Color Mode supports HDR color grading workflows, while the Clip Grid makes it easy to compare shots, identify inconsistencies, and navigate between clips that need additional adjustments.

Basic tools are also key

Sometimes you just need to get in and get out before publishing your video to social media. Adobe Premiere offers quick export options and simple editing tools.

Even simple adjustments can improve your video

Easily adjust color temperature, exposure, saturation, and more, much like editing a photo. Make adjustments to individual clips or across an entire sequence.

Adobe Premiere also offers Styles, which combine multiple color adjustments to help you quickly achieve a cohesive look across your footage.

The built-in Style Browser is full of presets that can help you achieve your desired color grading effect.

If you've achieved the perfect look in one clip, Adobe Premiere lets you easily copy that color grade and apply it to another, helping maintain visual consistency throughout a project.

Color grading tool pricing

Adobe Premiere offers far more than color grading. Its inclusion in the Adobe Creative Cloud Pro subscription gives you access to a comprehensive video editing platform alongside other creative apps, including Photoshop and After Effects.

While free online color grading tools may be sufficient for basic adjustments, some have limited export settings and color management capabilities. Professional software like Adobe Premiere gives you greater control over both the appearance and output quality of your footage.

Adobe's Creative Cloud Pro subscription, which includes Premiere and more than 20 creative apps, normally costs $69.99 per month. During Adobe's Black Friday sale, the price drops to $29.99 per month for the first year, reflecting a 57% discount.

Eligible students and teachers can save even more, with first-year pricing of $15.99 per month. Both promotional rates require an annual subscription billed monthly, with the offers ending Nov. 27.

With Adobe's Black Friday discount, now is an excellent time to invest in professional video editing and color grading software. Get Adobe Premiere through Creative Cloud Pro.

items.title: Best video compression software in 2026 - Adobe Premiere (Media Encoder) offers top video compression software
items.content_html:
Don't let poor video compression compromise your perfectly good footage. Instead, get the best video compression on export by using Adobe Premiere.

Video files can be large, especially when they're recorded at high resolutions and bit depths. Much of the detail and color information captured by your state-of-the-art iPhone camera can be lost through excessive compression when sharing footage on social media.

Get Adobe Premiere

You can preserve a lot of detail and color depth without exceeding upload limits by using a quality video compression tool. The best professional-grade tool available to compress video files is Adobe Premiere — whether you're a pro or not doesn't matter.

Manage file size from the start

Motion, image noise, and the quality of the recording environment can all influence how efficiently your video can be compressed. Before even considering a video compression tool, consider your workflow.

Good lighting can reduce image noise, and a tripod can minimize camera shake. Both can help video compression tools work more efficiently, preserving more detail without unnecessarily increasing file size.

Also, be aware of the format you're shooting in. Capturing more image data during recording can give you greater flexibility during editing and help improve the quality of your final export.

However, too much data can be a double-edged sword. If your workflow doesn't call for the additional flexibility that Apple ProRes offers during editing and color grading, recording in HEVC may be a more practical choice that saves considerable storage space.

Adobe Premiere is the best video compressor

Adobe Premiere can take your 4K HDR video recording and export it at 1080p for YouTube or other social media platforms. By adjusting the resolution, bitrate, and color space, you can significantly reduce file size while preserving as much detail and color fidelity as possible.

Adobe Premiere also integrates with Adobe Media Encoder, allowing you to queue multiple exports with different compression settings while continuing to edit. This is particularly useful when creating multiple versions of the same video for different social media platforms.

Adobe Premiere offers a range of export options to minimize quality loss

Poor compression tools often introduce artifacts into the video that obscure details and blur elements. While there are plenty of free options for handling video compression, Adobe Premiere combines professional-grade encoding tools with a comprehensive video editing workflow, giving you greater control over the finished product.

Adobe Premiere is the best video compressor for:

  • YouTube
  • Instagram
  • X
  • Email

Edit and export your video with Adobe Premiere using the appropriate compression and export settings for your intended platform. While social media services may still re-encode your footage, optimizing the file beforehand can help minimize unnecessary quality loss and reduce upload times.

By handling compression locally with Adobe Premiere, you can spend less time uploading large video files.

Video compression tool pricing

Adobe Premiere may be able to export your video with minimal compression loss at small file sizes, but it can do much more. Its inclusion in the Adobe Creative Cloud package means you get access to everything it can do, plus tons of other Adobe apps.

Rather than relying solely on the compression tools built into social media platforms, Adobe Premiere gives you control over the settings used to export your video. You can fine-tune export resolution, bitrate, and encoding options to strike the right balance between file size and visual quality.

Adobe Premiere is included in Adobe Creative Cloud Pro, which normally costs $69.99 per month for individuals. As part of Adobe's Black Friday promotion, the subscription is discounted to $29.99 per month for the first year, a savings of 57%.

items.title: Limited-edition 20th anniversary iPhone could be ceramic
items.content_html:
A new rumor from a leaker with a mixed track record claims that the iPhone 20 Pro will at least have ceramic components, and that's not the just existing Ceramic Shield display.

The most consistent rumor regarding the iPhone 20 Pro is that its design will resemble the iPhone Air, but with yet more rounded glass. Now leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Chinese social media site Weibo says that there will be ceramic components.

There are no details at all over what the components are, but they would presumably be an external feature. So it could be the whole chassis, or maybe a region that protects the USB-C port and speakers.

As noted by MacRumors, which first spotted the report, the leaker does say that Apple is not planning large-scale manufacturing. That suggests that ceramic might be used in a limited-edition iPhone 20 Pro.

The current iPhone Air does have versions of the Ceramic Shield on the front and back. So this rumor would fit with the earlier claim that the iPhone 20 Pro design would resemble the iPhone Air.

However, the leaker claims to have actually seen and handled components that they say are ceramic. That suggests that it will be more visibly ceramic than the Ceramic Shield, and perhaps be used as significantly as on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Conceivably, the new report concerns just another variation on this, especially as some rumors claim the chassis will be titanium. Although it was previously rumored that the iPhone 18 Pro would switch to titanium, and that didn't happen.

Note that Fixed Focus Digital is a leaker on Weibo. Generally leakers on that platform are less accurate, and more likely to repeat other rumors whether unfounded or not.

items.title: iOS 28 will either fix notification abuse or make it all worse
items.content_html:
Apple is reportedly planning to revamp how iPhone notifications work in iOS 28, although with no further details, it can only be hoped that it will be an improvement.

Let's not over-state this, because it's annoying but not exactly the end of the world. Apple will sometimes send notifications to your iPhone that are simply advertisements, but a sparse rumor about iOS 28 claims this could change.

The rumor is solely that Apple will make some significant changes to notifications. There is no clue whether this means reducing ads, increasing them, or just changing the color of the alerts.

So there is no evidence that it will change anything significant here. But the fact that this is the first thing some people think of, is a clue that ads like the "F1: The Movie" ticket offer have grated.

Any developer, not just Apple, can send iPhone notification ads, but in theory only if the user has expressly agreed to receive them. Only, as spotted by MacRumors which also reported on the iOS 28 rumor, that agreement isn't necessary.

Users report multiple cases where they have an app that has a setting to turn off these ads, but ignore it. There is also an overall App Store setting that means you can:

  • Open the App Store
  • Tap your profile photo
  • Choose Notifications
  • Turn off Recommendations & Offers

Yet allegedly, this setting is sometimes ignored too. It may be that it isn't ignored per se, though, it could be that the app manages to persuade a user to turn permission back on.

For instance, a delivery app could seemingly ask permission to update you on the current order. But then the developer chooses to interpret that as permission to continue all ads.

It seems unlikely that developers could just choose to ignore an App Store setting. But then it's also alleged that Apple itself is ignoring the rules it imposes on other developers.

In that case, it's probably that there is something in those terms and conditions of your iPhone or iOS that accepting them means allowing Apple to advertise.

Nonetheless, the notification ads keep coming. So the optics are poor for Apple, and that would suggest that it might do something to improve the matter.

But although, again, it's not as if Apple pushes an Apple Arcade game every twenty minutes, the optics aren't great. However it's hard to imagine what Apple could do that it isn't already doing, other than perhaps police the App Store better.

Still, since iOS 26, Apple Wallet has included a notifications setting too. In Wallet, tap the ellipses button, you can choose Notifications, then turn off New Features & Updates.

There's actually no way to force an Apple ad to appear as a test, so it's not clear whether the Wallet and App Store settings will turn off every such notification. But it's a start, and possibly Apple will do more with iOS 28, although it also expanding its use of advertising everywhere else.

items.title: AI chatbot companion app Talkie pulled from Apple App Store after investigation
items.content_html:
Apple says the Talkie app was removed from the App Store Wednesday due to sexual content, but a report suggests the violations go much further than that and involved minors.

So-called artificial intelligence can't think or reason, so when told to engage in roleplay it usually will without the right safeguards. Some apps that are easily found on the App Store are designed explicitly for roleplay, but tend to be locked behind age gates.

As some parents and an investigation from The Bureau of Investigative Journalism discovered, whether these apps are rated 18+ or require age verification, kids often find a way and encounter abusive or sexual content. The report led to an App Store removal according to South China Morning Post, first reported by 9to5Mac, though Apple says it did so due to sexual content and not abuse and use by minors.

The investigative report covers instances from December 2024 and doesn't specify if the children having inappropriate chats used iPhones, iPads, or Android devices. It also isn't clear why the story about events in 2024 was published today, nor why Apple was only alerted to these events upon publication.

AI is a wild west of unknowns and potential dangers. The App Store is full of apps for interacting with AI, and not all of them are 18+.

Even though Talkie was removed from the App Store, it remains accessible through the web and Google Play. Users can create their own characters to roleplay with and submit them for public use, and some of these characters are purpose-built for romantic or abusive relationships.

The AI genie is out of the bottle, so it is a tough world for parents to navigate, especially in situations where parents like ones in the investigation weren't aware of their child's access to a smartphone. Beyond age verification, age gating, and using parental control features, parents need to have frank discussions with their children about the dangers of engaging with AI chatbots.

Regulators are attempting to restrict access to AI companion apps and other such tools, but it's a losing battle so far. These products are so widely available and accessible, they're difficult to control.

Apple has its own AI called Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, but it won't roleplay with the user. It isn't an option and there's no convincing it or tricking it otherwise.

Talkie is owned and operated by a Hong Kong-based company called MiniMax. The company declined to comment on the situation.

items.title: AirFly Drive review: excellent wireless CarPlay for one driver, not two
items.content_html:
Twelve South has surpassed many previous wireless CarPlay adapters with its AirFly Drive, and also beaten them on price, but it can get fiddly when more than one person uses it.

Your car may already support wireless CarPlay, in which case the odds are you know it because you'll have already been prompted to turn it on. If you use a wired connection, though, AirFly Drive is a very tempting adapter.

Where you ordinarily plug your cable in, you instead plug the AirFly Drive and leave it there. Then once it has been paired with your iPhone, everything works exactly as if it is the phone that is wired in.

So your car's infotainment screen becomes an Apple CarPlay one with Maps, Music, Phone, and countless more options. All of which are better done than most car manufacturer's systems, or else you wouldn't bother.

AirFly Drive review: a worthy overall package

Traditionally, one reason not to buy a CarPlay adapter has been that they are expensive. And another is that they can be rubbish with dropped connections, long delays as you press buttons, and so on.

Twelve South hasn't fixed the latency issue, but it's minor, and it's also consistent. When you're playing music, for instance, it tends to take around three seconds to stop when you've pressed pause.

That's because the press has to be detected and then the pause action be relayed back to your iPhone wirelessly. It would be great if there were no delay, especially since that's what you would be used to if you had wired CarPlay.

But since it is always the same amount of time, you get used to it.

Twelve South has, though, fixed the price. This is just $40.

AirFly Drive review: what you get and setting up

In the packaging, you get instructions plus this very tiny AirFly Drive. The device has a USB-A connector which will fit most cars, but there's also a USB-C adapter in the box.

It's powered from your car, so the first time when you plug AirFly Drive in and turn on the ignition, your infotainment screen switches to show setup instructions. Those boil down to you pairing the device to your phone, and then in theory, that's it.

AirFly Drive has a USB-A plug but the company also provides a USB-C adapter.

In practice, it certainly is it so long as you are the only user. From now on, when you turn on the ignition, you have CarPlay even though your iPhone might be in your pocket.

Actually, even if you're still walking up to your car, there can be enough of a connection that suddenly your pocket is playing out Sheryl Crow at full volume. But get into the car, turn the ignition, and she's now coming through your car's speakers perfectly.

All of this was flawless and actually exciting in AppleInsider testing. I bought this specifically because I was buying an iPhone Duo and didn't want to chuck that costly device into a gap below my dashboard like I used to with my old iPhone.

But as well as no longer fearing that I'd scrape or scratch my iPhone, I've really enjoyed the instantaneous starting. And it's deeply enjoyable how you can be surrounded by music without doing anything.

There are two situations, though, where the enjoyment gets a bit tarnished. That's not to say that it's the AirFly Drive's fault, but it doesn't help.

AirFly Drive review: using navigation

I use Apple Maps in CarPlay and most of the time, there hasn't been a problem. It has just worked as it always did, it has worked exactly as well as if I still had my iPhone wired in.

Only, if I had the iPhone in my jeans pocket and if I were also driving through a city, there were definitely problems. Apple Maps would go crazy trying to figure out where I was or comparing the turn I appeared to be making to what turn was actually possible.

AirFly Drive is very easy to setup and this screen couldn't be simpler. But still, you keep seeing it even after you have set up your iPhone.

Over and over, the map would flap around between different streets, or throw up that "Proceed to the route."

You don't want to be fiddling around while driving, so when this happens I would switch to my car's own map system. And realise anew why I use CarPlay.

To be fair to Twelve South, this is about GPS signal strength and my choice of clothing. Plus it didn't take long to realise that it was signal blocking that was causing the problem.

But it did take longer than it should, because of a second issue.

AirFly Drive review: two users are tricky

In theory, AirFly Drive can be paired to two iPhones. The idea is that when you get into the car, it tries to connect to whichever one used it last.

If it fails, because that iPhone isn't there, it then switches to try the other of the two you've set up. It's supposed to take between 15 and 30 seconds to go through this, or you can press the device's one button to make it switch immediately.

Every time I pressed that button I seemed to reset the whole device.

Or it would appear as if I had, because sometimes the initial setup screen would return. Whether I press the button or on occasion just if I get into my car with my paired iPhone, I may see that setup screen.

What I thought was happening is that this screen is shown while the AirFly Drive is looking for a previously-connected iPhone. That could well be the case and I think it certainly was the first several times it happened, but it isn't consistent.

Still, whatever causes that setup screen to appear, do nothing. If you don't try setting up anything again, and if you don't press that button, in a very few seconds, it finds your iPhone and all is well.

Or nearly.

Once when I was having that jeans- and city-related trouble with navigating, my wife started the same route on her iPhone. After a moment, she was seeing the same map-flipping confusion.

But she had her iPhone in her hand. And what was actually happening was that AirFly Drive had switched back to my phone.

Since I'd not gone into my pocket to stop Apple Maps, the route on our car's screen was the same. There was just no clue that it had swapped until I tried coming out of Maps and saw my apps instead of hers.

A blue light tells you the AirFly Drive is connected to your iPhone.

Now when I'm driving alone, I've got used to it taking a time to realise it's my iPhone. And everything I enjoyed about wireless CarPlay at first is still great, as long as I don't leave my phone in my jeans.

But when my wife is driving, she just pulls out the AirFly Drive and reconnects her iPhone by cable. That does also give her the advantage that when we get somewhere, her iPhone is fully charged.

AirFly Drive review: Should you buy

For the first few days when I was driving with it solely paired to my iPhone, I'd have instantly said yes. And since I didn't happen to hit the maps problem at first, and since the delay in pressing buttons didn't bother me, I might have given this 5 stars.

I still think that what it does, it does very, very well. Plus I am conscious that some of the problems I've had were down to my dress sense and also my hurried use of it when I was late driving somewhere.

Given that it can still be confusing when you get a setup screen for what you've already set up, I want to step down to 4. It takes more getting used to than you might expect from what is seemingly such a simple device.

Yet it is simple, it does just plug in, and once you're paired, it does (usually) just work. I've long enjoyed CarPlay and I wouldn't now buy a car that didn't have it, but I am enjoying and appreciating it anew because of the Twelve South AirFly Drive.

AirFly Drive review: Pros

  • Simple to install
  • Works great for one user
  • Inexpensive

AirFly Drive review: Cons

  • Two-user switching takes getting used to
  • Three-second delay on CarPlay buttons
  • Phone can't be shielded too much, or Maps doesn't work right

Rating: 4 out of 5

AirFly Drive review: Where to Buy

AirFly Drive is available in either white or black directly from Twelve South for $39.99.

It's typically available on Amazon for $31.99.

items.title: What to watch for after the new 1Password data breach
items.content_html:
1Password is warning customers to watch for phishing scams after an attacker used an employee's GitHub account to steal customer records.

An attacker breached 1Password's backend systems and copied customer names, email addresses, and other account data. The company said customer vaults, their contents, and the keys protecting them were unaffected.

According to 1Password, an investigation began on November 19, 2026, after 1Password detected signs that someone had accessed an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker copied private source code and used the account to push malicious code that extracted customer records.

Stolen records include account IDs, sign-in times, and tokens embedded in some invitation and recovery links. The company says that users who's data was stolen have been emailed. It's not clear how many notifications went out.

Additionally, the company disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked or rotated potentially exposed credentials, and lengthened invitation and recovery codes. It said services were operating normally and found no evidence of customer account takeovers.

Customers don't need to change their account settings, but 1Password advises watching for unexpected invitations and recovery requests. Be wary of requests, and enter credentials only in the official app or on the website you open directly.

Report suspicious messages to support@1password.com.
